dryRun.title: What each line does
rows: allowed (binding is fixed, object is not)
dryRun.note: const fixes the binding, not the value. You cannot point the name at something else, but you can still change the object it points to.

think.q:
if (true) { var a = 1; let b = 2 }
console.log(typeof a, typeof b)
why: var ignores the block and lives in the whole function (here the whole script). let stays inside { }, so outside it b does not exist and typeof gives "undefined".
think.exec:
if (true) { var a = 1; let b = 2 }
console.log(typeof a, typeof b)

think.q:
const user = { name: 'A' }
user.name = 'B'
console.log(user.name)
why: const stops you reassigning user, not changing its properties. The object is still mutable.
To freeze the object too, use Object.freeze(user).

think.q: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
why: There is only one var i for the whole loop. When the timeouts run, the loop has finished and i is 3.
With let each iteration gets its own i, so it prints 0 1 2.
think.exec: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i))

think.q: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
why: let in a for loop creates a fresh binding per iteration, so each callback remembers its own value.
think.exec: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i))

think.q: Which should you use by default for a new variable?
why: Start with const. Switch to let only when you really reassign. var is legacy.
Reading const tells the next person "this name never points elsewhere".

try.task: Write makeCounters(n) that returns an array of n functions; the i-th function returns i. It must work with a normal for loop.
try.hint: Use let in the loop header so every function captures its own i.

checks.t: each function returns its own index

takeaway.key: Use const by default, let when you reassign, never var. const fixes the name, not the object.
mistakes: Thinking const makes an object immutable.
Using var in a loop with callbacks: all of them see the last value.
Reading a let before its line: that is the TDZ, a ReferenceError.

dryRun.title: Copying a primitive vs copying an object
dryRun.note: Primitives (number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint) are copied by value. Objects, arrays and functions are copied by reference: both names point at the same thing.

think.q:
let x = { n: 1 }
let y = x
y.n = 2
console.log(x.n)
why: y = x copies the reference, so both names share one object.
think.exec:
let x = { n: 1 }
let y = x
y.n = 2
console.log(x.n)

think.q: console.log([1] === [1], 'a' === 'a')
why: Two array literals are two different objects, so === compares references and says false. Strings are primitives and compare by value.

think.q: console.log(typeof null, typeof [], typeof function () {})
why: typeof null is "object": a famous bug from JavaScript's first version that can never be fixed.
Arrays are objects; use Array.isArray. Functions are the one object type typeof reports separately.
think.exec: console.log(typeof null, typeof [], typeof function () {})

think.q:
function f(o) { o.n = 9; o = { n: 0 } }
const obj = { n: 1 }
f(obj)
console.log(obj.n)
why: Inside f, o starts as a copy of the reference, so o.n = 9 changes the shared object. Then o = {...} only re-points the local name.
JavaScript always passes by value; for objects the value is a reference.

think.q: You want a copy of { a: 1, tags: ["x"] } where changing copy.tags does not change the original. What do you use?
why: Spread and Object.assign make a shallow copy: tags is still shared.
structuredClone makes a deep copy (built into browsers and Node 17+).

try.task: Write isPrimitive(value): true for the 7 primitive types, false for objects, arrays and functions. Careful with null.
try.hint: A value is an object if typeof is "object" or "function", except null.

checks.t: numbers, strings, undefined, symbols, bigints are primitive
objects, arrays and functions are not

takeaway.key: Primitives are copied by value; objects by reference. Two names can share one object, and === on objects compares identity, not contents.
mistakes: Expecting { ...obj } to deep-copy nested objects.
Trusting typeof x === "object" without excluding null.
Comparing arrays or objects with === to check equal contents.

dryRun.title: Which fallback wins?
dryRun.note: || falls back on any falsy value. ?? falls back only on null or undefined, so real values like 0 and "" survive.

think.q:
const n = 0
console.log(n || 10, n ?? 10)
why: || treats 0 as falsy and falls back. ?? only falls back on null/undefined, so 0 stays.
think.exec:
const n = 0
console.log(n || 10, n ?? 10)

think.q:
const user = {}
console.log(user.address?.city, user.getName?.())
why: ?. stops and returns undefined as soon as the left side is null or undefined, instead of throwing.
think.exec:
const user = {}
console.log(user.address?.city, user.getName?.())

think.q: console.log(NaN === NaN, Number.isNaN(NaN), isNaN('abc'))
why: NaN is the only value not equal to itself. Number.isNaN checks for real NaN. The old global isNaN first converts: "abc" becomes NaN, so it says true.
think.exec: console.log(NaN === NaN, Number.isNaN(NaN), isNaN('abc'))

think.q:
let a
const b = null
console.log(a == b, a === b, typeof a, typeof b)
why: == treats null and undefined as equal to each other (and to nothing else). === does not. typeof null is "object".
think.exec:
let a
const b = null
console.log(a == b, a === b, typeof a, typeof b)

think.q: What is the difference in intent between undefined and null?
opts: null is for numbers, undefined for strings
undefined is an error, null is not
undefined: no value was ever set. null: someone deliberately set "no value".
why: Missing properties, missing arguments and uninitialised variables are undefined. You write null on purpose.

try.task: Write getSetting(config, key, fallback): return config[key] unless it is null or undefined (or config itself is missing), else the fallback. 0, false and "" are real values.

checks.verify: assert(getSetting({ a: 0 }, "a", 9) === 0 && getSetting({ a: false }, "a", 9) === false && getSetting({ a: "" }, "a", 9) === "", "falsy values must be kept")

checks.t: a missing config does not throw

takeaway.key: Use ?? for defaults and ?. for maybe-missing paths. Check NaN with Number.isNaN.
mistakes: Using || for defaults and losing a real 0 or "".
Checking x === NaN: it is always false.
Using global isNaN("abc") and getting true for a string.

dryRun.title: How + decides
dryRun.note: + concatenates if either side is (or becomes) a string. Every other arithmetic operator converts both sides to numbers.

think.q: console.log('5' + 3, '5' - 3, '5' * '2')
why: + with a string concatenates: "53". Minus and times only work on numbers, so "5" becomes 5.

think.q: console.log(JSON.stringify([] + []), [] + {}, 1 + null, 1 + undefined)
why: Arrays become strings: [] → "". Objects become "[object Object]". null becomes 0, undefined becomes NaN.
think.exec: console.log(JSON.stringify([] + []), [] + {}, 1 + null, 1 + undefined)

think.q: console.log(Boolean(''), Boolean('0'), Boolean([]), Boolean(0))
why: Only 8 falsy values exist: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. The string "0" and an empty array are truthy.
think.exec: console.log(Boolean(''), Boolean('0'), Boolean([]), Boolean(0))

think.q: console.log(Number(''), Number(' 42 '), Number('4x'), parseInt('4x'))
why: Number converts the whole string (spaces trimmed, empty → 0) and fails with NaN on any junk. parseInt reads digits until it hits junk.
think.exec: console.log(Number(''), Number(' 42 '), Number('4x'), parseInt('4x'))

think.q: A form gives "10" and "5". total = a + b shows 105. Fix?
why: Convert explicitly at the boundary where the data comes in.
a - -b happens to work but nobody reading it knows why.

try.task: Write toNumberStrict(value): return a number for a number or a numeric string (spaces allowed), else null. Empty or blank strings, booleans, arrays and null give null.
try.hint: Reject non-strings/non-numbers first, then blank strings, then use Number and Number.isNaN.

checks.t: junk, booleans, arrays and null give null
checks.verify: assert([ "4x", true, [], null, undefined, NaN ].every((v) => toNumberStrict(v) === null), "junk")

takeaway.key: + concatenates if either side is a string; other operators convert to numbers. Convert explicitly with Number() / String() / Boolean().
mistakes: Adding form input strings with +.
Thinking "0" or [] is falsy.
Number("") is 0, not NaN.

dryRun.title: What == does before comparing
dryRun.note: === never converts: different types are simply not equal. == converts first, with special rules. Use ===, except x == null as a short "null or undefined" check.

think.q: console.log(0 == '', 0 === '', null == 0, null == undefined)
why: "" becomes 0 under ==, so true. Strict equality says different types, false. null equals only undefined under ==.
think.exec: console.log(0 == '', 0 === '', null == 0, null == undefined)

think.q: console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN), Object.is(0, -0), 0 === -0)
why: Object.is is "same value": NaN equals NaN, and 0 and -0 are different. === says the opposite for both.
think.exec: console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN), Object.is(0, -0), 0 === -0)

think.q:
const a = { id: 1 }, b = { id: 1 }
console.log(a == b, a === b, a === a)
why: Objects compare by identity with both operators. Same contents, different objects: false.
think.exec:
const a = { id: 1 }, b = { id: 1 }
console.log(a == b, a === b, a === a)

think.q: console.log([1, NaN].includes(NaN), [1, NaN].indexOf(NaN))
why: includes uses SameValueZero, which finds NaN. indexOf uses ===, which never matches NaN.
think.exec: console.log([1, NaN].includes(NaN), [1, NaN].indexOf(NaN))

think.q: Which use of == is a common, accepted idiom?
why: x == null is true exactly for null and undefined. Everything else should use ===.

try.task: Write shallowEqual(a, b): true when two plain objects have the same keys and each value is Object.is-equal (one level only).
try.hint: Compare key counts first, then every key with Object.is. Use Object.hasOwn so a missing key does not match an undefined value.

checks.t: same keys and values are equal
checks.verify: assert(shallowEqual({ a: 1, b: "x" }, { b: "x", a: 1 }) === true, "equal")
const o = {}; assert(shallowEqual({ a: {} }, { a: {} }) === false && shallowEqual({ a: o }, { a: o }) === true, "reference")

checks.t: NaN equals NaN, extra or missing keys differ
checks.verify: assert(shallowEqual({ a: NaN }, { a: NaN }) === true && shallowEqual({ a: 1 }, { a: 1, b: 2 }) === false && shallowEqual({ a: undefined }, { b: undefined }) === false, "edge")

takeaway.key: Use ===. It never converts. The one accepted == is x == null. Objects compare by identity.
mistakes: Expecting two objects with the same contents to be ===.
Finding NaN with indexOf; use includes or Number.isNaN.
Relying on == rules like 0 == "".

problems.name: To Be Or Not To Be

dryRun.title: const { a, b: { c } = {}, ...rest } = obj
rows: obj.b.c (b itself is not a variable)
dryRun.note: Destructuring pulls values out by name (objects) or position (arrays). Defaults apply only when the value is undefined, not null.

think.q:
const { a = 5, b = 5 } = { a: null }
console.log(a, b)
why: Defaults kick in only for undefined. a is null, which is a real value, so the default is skipped.
think.exec:
const { a = 5, b = 5 } = { a: null }
console.log(a, b)

think.q:
const [x, , y = 9, ...rest] = [1, 2, undefined, 4, 5]
console.log(x, y, rest)
why: The empty slot skips 2. The third item is undefined, so the default 9 applies. ...rest collects what is left.
think.exec:
const [x, , y = 9, ...rest] = [1, 2, undefined, 4, 5]
console.log(x, y, rest)

think.q:
const a = { x: 1, inner: { y: 2 } }
const b = { ...a }
b.inner.y = 99
console.log(a.inner.y)
why: Spread copies one level. inner is the same object in both.

think.q:
let p = 1, q = 2;
[p, q] = [q, p]
console.log(p, q)
why: Array destructuring swaps two variables without a temp. Note the semicolon before the line starting with [.

think.q: Which signature lets callers pass options in any order and skip the whole object?
why: Destructured params with defaults read like named arguments. The trailing = {} makes f() work without an argument.

try.task: Write pick(obj, keys) that returns a new object with only the listed keys that exist in obj, and omit(obj, keys) that returns everything else.
try.hint: For omit, copy with spread, then delete the keys. For pick, loop over keys and use Object.hasOwn.

checks.t: pick keeps only listed, existing keys

checks.verify: const o = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const p = pick(o, ["a"]), r = omit(o, ["a"]); assert(p && r && r.b === 2 && o.a === 1 && o.b === 2 && p !== o && r !== o, "input changed or no new object")

takeaway.key: Destructure by name or position, defaults apply only to undefined, and spread/rest copy just one level.
mistakes: Expecting a default for a null value.
Thinking { ...obj } copies nested objects.
Forgetting = {} on a destructured parameter, so calling with no argument throws.

dryRun.title: new Map() vs a plain object as a dictionary
dryRun.note: Use Map when keys are dynamic or not strings; use Set for unique values. A plain object is best for fixed, known fields.

think.q:
const o = {}
const k1 = { id: 1 }, k2 = { id: 2 }
o[k1] = 'a'; o[k2] = 'b'
console.log(Object.keys(o).length, o[k1])
why: Both object keys become the same string "[object Object]", so the second write overwrites the first.
A Map would keep both keys.

think.q:
const s = new Set([1, 1, '1', NaN, NaN])
console.log(s.size)
why: Set uses SameValueZero: duplicate 1 removed, "1" is a different value, and NaN counts once.
think.exec:
const s = new Set([1, 1, '1', NaN, NaN])
console.log(s.size)

think.q:
const m = new Map([['b', 2], ['a', 1]])
m.set('c', 3)
console.log([...m.keys()].join(''))
why: Map iterates in insertion order. It never sorts keys.

think.q:
const s = new Set([{ a: 1 }])
console.log(s.has({ a: 1 }))
why: A Set compares objects by identity, like ===. A new object literal is a different object.
think.exec:
const s = new Set([{ a: 1 }])
console.log(s.has({ a: 1 }))

think.q: You need to remove duplicates from an array of strings, keeping first-seen order. Simplest?
why: A Set keeps the first of each value in insertion order, and spreading it back gives an array.

try.task: Write groupCount(words): return a Map from each word to how many times it appears, in first-seen order.

checks.verify: assert(groupCount(["a"]) instanceof Map, "must be a Map")

takeaway.key: Map for dynamic or non-string keys, Set for uniqueness. Both keep insertion order and compare objects by identity.
mistakes: Using objects as keys in a plain object: they all become "[object Object]".
Expecting set.has({...}) to match an equal-looking object.

dryRun.title: JSON.stringify({ a: 1, f() {}, u: undefined, d: new Date(0), n: NaN, m: new Map([[1, 2]]) })
dryRun.note: JSON knows only strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. Everything else is dropped, turned into null, or turned into something lossy. Round-tripping through JSON is not a safe clone.

think.q: console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: null }))
why: Object properties holding undefined or functions are skipped. null is kept.
think.exec: console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: null }))

think.q: console.log(JSON.stringify([undefined, () => 1, NaN]))
why: Inside arrays they cannot be skipped (positions matter), so they become null.
think.exec: console.log(JSON.stringify([undefined, () => 1, NaN]))

think.q:
const d = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ when: new Date(0) }))
console.log(typeof d.when)
why: The Date became a string on the way out, and JSON.parse does not turn it back. Use a reviver if you need a Date again.
think.exec:
const d = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ when: new Date(0) }))
console.log(typeof d.when)

think.q: console.log(JSON.stringify({ b: 1, a: [1, 2] }, null, 0) === JSON.stringify({ b: 1, a: [1, 2] }), JSON.stringify({ x: 1 }, ['x', 'y']))
why: A space argument of 0 adds no whitespace, so the strings are identical. An array as the second argument is an allow-list of keys.
think.exec: console.log(JSON.stringify({ b: 1, a: [1, 2] }, null, 0) === JSON.stringify({ b: 1, a: [1, 2] }), JSON.stringify({ x: 1 }, ['x', 'y']))

think.q: JSON.stringify(obj) throws "Converting circular structure to JSON". What does it mean?
opts: Some object inside refers back to an ancestor, so the output would be infinite
why: Functions and undefined are silently dropped. Only cycles (and BigInt) throw.

try.task: Write reviveDates(json): parse a JSON string and turn every string that looks like an ISO date (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss...Z) back into a Date, at any depth.
try.hint: JSON.parse takes a second argument: (key, value) => newValue, called for every value, deepest first.

checks.verify: const r = reviveDates('{"at":"2026-01-02T03:04:05.000Z"}'); assert(r.at instanceof Date && r.at.getUTCFullYear() === 2026, "date")

takeaway.key: JSON keeps strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. Functions/undefined vanish, NaN becomes null, Dates become strings. Use a reviver to restore types.
mistakes: Cloning with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) and losing Dates, Maps and undefined.
Expecting a Date back after parse.
